speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM TARGET FOR RATE OF INFLATION IN 1977-REASON FOR DELAYING BUDGET-DURATION OF CONTROL PERIOD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. The other day in the House I directed a question to the minister about the government's inflation targets for 1977. At that time the minister stated that his hopes of achieving their targets, and I think I quote him, were tempered by some of the difficulties of the economic situation. Since we now have a CPI increase of almost one per cent in January, the largest jump in some 13 or 14 months, is the minister prepared to give the country and the House some clear indication of the inflation targets for 1977 of the government of Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM TARGET FOR RATE OF INFLATION IN 1977-REASON FOR DELAYING BUDGET-DURATION OF CONTROL PERIOD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would point out that on the year-over-year basis, the rate is at 6.1 per cent. As I indicated in my speech yesterday, and have on many previous occasions, we would anticipate that through 1977 there may be some increase in the consumer price index, but we are confident that we can bring that level down to the target which has been set out for some 15 months of 6 per cent by the end of 1977.1 have to say that the prospects of getting below the 6 per cent rate in the current calendar year are difficult, but of course that does remain a target. We anticipate that there will be some increase in food prices, and other price elements in the consumer price index will not be coming down as quickly. But the target, which I have stated a number of times, of 6 per cent by the end of 1977 remains attainable, and depending on economic circumstances we are still hopeful we might go below that.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM TARGET FOR RATE OF INFLATION IN 1977-REASON FOR DELAYING BUDGET-DURATION OF CONTROL PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, clearly one of the factors upon which that will depend is government policy. Will the minister give the House some indication of when we can expect to have a budget from the government, and if it will not be in the next
February 11, 1977

two to three weeks, will he tell us why he is delaying the introduction of a budget in a period when the CPI is going up, when unemployment is going up, and when the controls regime is clearly forcing a diversion of investment out of the country?

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM TARGET FOR RATE OF INFLATION IN 1977-REASON FOR DELAYING BUDGET-DURATION OF CONTROL PERIOD
speechtext: It seems to me that the last comment is without substantial foundation whatsoever. The government has indicated very strongly its policy with regard to inflation, that is to restrain the increase of expenditure at the public level, in support of the Bank of Canada to restrain the growth of the monetary mass in Canada, and, above all, to maintain the program of controls for the purpose of bringing down the increases in the consumer price index. I am now in the process of preparation and am indeed in pre-budget consultation and I will be indicating to the House, probably within a couple of weeks, the time in the next several months when we propose to make a budget presentation.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM TARGET FOR RATE OF INFLATION IN 1977-REASON FOR DELAYING BUDGET-DURATION OF CONTROL PERIOD
speechtext: Did I understand the minister correctly to say that part of the program of the government is to maintain the controls, and if that is what the minister said, can he give the House some indication of how long the government intends to maintain the program of controls and when we might have a specific indication in that regard?

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM TARGET FOR RATE OF INFLATION IN 1977-REASON FOR DELAYING BUDGET-DURATION OF CONTROL PERIOD
speechtext: I have responded extensively on this point. The intention would be to maintain the controls for the year 1977, unless we can expect from major decision makers in the economy some strong commitment and support to restrain the kind of inflationary increases which might occur if the control program were taken off prematurely. This is the statement I have made on a number of occasions both in and out of the House.

REASON FOR PERMITTING GROWTH IN GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES-REASON FOR FAILURE TO REDUCE SALES TAX
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of Finance. As the minister has indicated that it is government policy to restrain spending at the government level, which this week was indicated to be up again by 11 per cent in the coming fiscal year, would the minister indicate, if his target of a 6 per cent inflation in the current year is to be met with a real growth at 3.5 per cent, why is government spending contemplated to go up by 11 per cent, which would appear to be 1.5 per cent greater than the growth in the GNP?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: REASON FOR PERMITTING GROWTH IN GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES-REASON FOR FAILURE TO REDUCE SALES TAX
speechtext: We have systematically set for ourselves a program over a period of time to reduce the percentage of the GNP that the government of Canada takes. I expect we will meet the target for the fiscal year 1976-77. We have set a lower target for 1977-78 and we expect to be able to meet it. Obviously, economic circumstances may vary within a year. It is important in expenditure planning to have longer term targets and systematic planning.

subtopic: REASON FOR PERMITTING GROWTH IN GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES-REASON FOR FAILURE TO REDUCE SALES TAX
speechtext:

REASON FOR DIFFERENCE BETWEEN CANADIAN AND UNITED STATES RATES OF INFLATION
speechtext: The minister referred to the current CPI figure in Canada. Would he indicate why, with controls, we are not doing as well in controlling inflation in Canada as they are in the United States without controls, where the over-all price increase based on total expenditures is 4.8 per cent compared with the 9 per cent increase in Canada?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. Since the major reason for the increase in the consumer price index is the 1.2 per cent increase in the cost of food, including almost all food items, and since the cabinet received a recommendation, I understand, from its D.M.10 group at a cabinet meeting which took place in the first week of June last year that the government should prepare a comprehensive national food policy, I would like to ask the Prime Minister when we might expect such a comprehensive policy announcement from the government.

speechtext: Could the Prime Minister inform us when we might expect these particular enactments from the government? I am thinking of the fact that the controls program does not apply to most of the components which make up the consumer price index as it affects food, so I would like to ask the Prime Minister if the detailed announcements to which he refers will cover such items as energy costs and the cost of the implements which are used in the production of food. subtopic: DATE OF ANNOUNCEMENT OF FOOD POLICY AND ACTION TO DEAL WITH ITEMS RELATED TO FOOD PRODUCTION
speechtext: Some of the elements mentioned by the hon. member are controlled now. Energy, farm implements and the whole distribution and processing process are under the antiinflation guidelines now. As far as other policies are concerned, they will be announced from time to time.

subtopic: DATE OF ANNOUNCEMENT OF FOOD POLICY AND ACTION TO DEAL WITH ITEMS RELATED TO FOOD PRODUCTION
speechtext: Given the very real need for a comprehensive approach to food policy both from a consumer and a producer point of view, and given the need to meet in an honest way the difficult trade-offs which are involved, would the Prime Minister explain to the House why the cabinet turned down the recommendation it received from its senior group of civil servants last June to come forward with a comprehensive national food policy?

subtopic: DATE OF ANNOUNCEMENT OF FOOD POLICY AND ACTION TO DEAL WITH ITEMS RELATED TO FOOD PRODUCTION
speechtext: I am not aware that we turned down anything. We have been examining policies put forward by various departments and deputy ministers, and we have been adopting or modifying various elements of them.

subtopic: SUGGESTED ADOPTION OF NEW CONSUMER PRICE INDEX-ACTION TO STIMULATE ECONOMY
SUGGESTED ADOPTION OF NEW CONSUMER PRICE INDEX-ACTION TO STIMULATE ECONOMY
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Since, according to our analysis on this side of the House, our consumer price index takes into account only a very small percentage of the increase in prices, as compared with the index in the United States, and since the system here does not give us a comparable rate, when will a new index be used by the Canadian government, to show the people really how bad the situation is? And, in answering the hon. member for York-Simcoe, did the minister really believe that by controlling government expenditures and properly stimulating the private sector we would be increasing the inflation rate in this country? In other words, when are we going to have action from this government in the middle of a cold, sad winter?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: SUGGESTED ADOPTION OF NEW CONSUMER PRICE INDEX-ACTION TO STIMULATE ECONOMY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I repeat, effective as at the beginning of this year there has been, in substance, a $3 billion transfer in the direction of personal disposable incomes.

subtopic: SUGGESTED ADOPTION OF NEW CONSUMER PRICE INDEX-ACTION TO STIMULATE ECONOMY
speechtext: Oh! It was $1.7 billion yesterday.

subtopic: SUGGESTED ADOPTION OF NEW CONSUMER PRICE INDEX-ACTION TO STIMULATE ECONOMY
speechtext: I suggest to the hon. gentleman that the kinds of measures which his leader was suggesting yesterday are now operative in this economy. The suggestion that the hon. member has a new consumer price index, or a new statistical system which we should follow, I find interesting. It might be useful if he were to submit his findings to my colleague the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Statistics Canada might have something to say about it.

maintopic: ALLEGED HARDSHIP CAUSED SENIOR CITIZENS BY INDEXING PENSIONS ON BASIS OF CONSUMER PRICE INDEX-GOVERNMENT ACTION
ALLEGED HARDSHIP CAUSED SENIOR CITIZENS BY INDEXING PENSIONS ON BASIS OF CONSUMER PRICE INDEX-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I direct my question to the Minister of Finance. Having toured this country to learn the quality of life of our senior citizens, and noting that the food component of the consumer price index jumped upward 1.2 per cent in January, which caused the over-all consumer price index to rise by 0.9 per cent, the largest monthly increase since November, 1975, and noting as well that senior citizens of Canada will still lose part of their buying power for bare essentials, despite indexing, I ask if the minister is aware that old age security benefits as indexed through the consumer price index really do not assist senior citizens who are primarily interested in costs of food, clothing and housing? Will he admit that, for these people, the formula used is creating a hardship?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
maintopic: ALLEGED HARDSHIP CAUSED SENIOR CITIZENS BY INDEXING PENSIONS ON BASIS OF CONSUMER PRICE INDEX-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is difficult in a general consumer price index to make certain that it measures the demands of every-

one in the economy. I do not imagine that even the personal indexing system as proposed by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi would be able to satisfy that. The fact is, there will be some differences between the impacts on different groups in the community. I think it is fair to observe that if the food component is particularly important to this group, and it is important to all Canadians, that they have really been very much the beneficiaries of the very substantial drop in food prices which has occurred over the last ten months.

maintopic: ALLEGED HARDSHIP CAUSED SENIOR CITIZENS BY INDEXING PENSIONS ON BASIS OF CONSUMER PRICE INDEX-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Notwithstanding the minister's unacceptable answer and his belief that it is impossible to derive some formula which would assist our senior citizens, will the minister explore all avenues, in order to determine whether it is possible to introduce a better formula for indexing old age security pensions and thereby give our senior citizens a break?

maintopic: ALLEGED HARDSHIP CAUSED SENIOR CITIZENS BY INDEXING PENSIONS ON BASIS OF CONSUMER PRICE INDEX-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would be glad to discuss this with the Minister of National Health and Welfare. As for the food component, may I point out to the hon. gentleman again that it is below the level of one year ago.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed either to the Secretary of State for External Affairs or to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. In 1976, a permit to export 150 metric tons of crude cesium ore to the U.S.S.R was refused by ITC, although trade had taken place involving this commodity for the previous seven years. Is a ban now in effect on cesium exports and, if so, has action been taken to stockpile this valuable material in order that domestic research into its use as a catalyst to prolong the life of fossil fuel can be undertaken, thus creating employment, and especially allowing mines such as Tantalum Mines at Bernic Lake, Manitoba, to continue operations?
Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Secretary of State for External
Affairs): I recall hearing some months ago about the prohibition of this particular export. I am not in a position at the moment to say whether shipments have been resumed or whether the material is still on the restricted list but I will make inquiries and see what, if anything, can be done. My recollection is that cesium is regarded as being in the category of strategic materials but I will have to look into the matter more deeply.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the absence of the Minister of Agriculture and his parliamentary secretary, I shall put my question to the right hon. Prime Minister.
As the Minister of Urban Affairs admitted barely ten days ago on television that the government had erred in its dairy policy; as that policy has led to in the last year the disappearance of hundreds of dairy producers, specially in Quebec, and as the government has not agreed to absorb the cost of export costs as does the European Economic Community in the case of its dairy producers, I should like to ask the Prime Minister if, under those circumstances and bearing in mind the hardships of the dairy producers, he is willing to comply with the recommendations of the federation to the effect that the government absorb export costs which, in the main, caused most of the dairy producers' problems. speakeroldname: Hon. Ron Basford (Minister of Justice) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CANADIAN HUMAN RIGHTS ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROTECT PRIVACY OF INDIVIDUALS
speechtext:
that Bill C-25, to extend the present laws in Canada that proscribe discrimination and that protect the privacy of individuals, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of satisfaction that I see today the end of a period of frustration for me and other supporters of this bill as we open the debate on second reading of the Canadian Human Rights Act, Bill C-25. It is timely that we discuss this bill at this time and that we pass it as expeditiously as parliamentary procedures will allow. Throughout the country there has been considerable discussion of human rights matters. In this chamber the discussion has raised the broad issue of the rights of a citizen to have access to the personal information about himself or herself that is held by government departments or agencies.
Elsewhere, away from this House, there has also been voiced deep and urgent concern in various parts of the country about the extent of racism and other illegitimate forms of discrimination being practised in our country, and we see in the news media from time to time reports of nasty racial incidents which have occurred to an extent where one provincial government has found it necessary to appoint a royal commission on certain aspects of the problem. It is, therefore, a matter of some satisfaction for me to be able to rise and state that there is now a bill before parliament which addresses both these and other issues connected with human rights within federal jurisdiction and addresses them in a comprehensive legislative way.
I suspect there are many people in the country who imagine that there is no discrimination in Canada and no need to act. Sadly, however-I know members on all sides will agree with me-it is a fact that there are some among us who are prepared to subvert our basic values by denying the basic rights of others. Their activities are deplorable. But it is not enough for us in parliament to deplore. We must also act, and act so as to ensure that the confidence of minorities in the protection afforded by the law is honoured and upheld.
Of course, no single piece of legislation can automatically, at the stroke of a pen, wipe out racism and discrimination overnight or change deepseated social attitudes, prejudices or hatreds. But without this bill at the federal level, victims of racist activities or of discrimination can point to the absence of a federal law and ask: Where is this country's, or this parliament's commitment to uphold tolerance, and where is this country's, or this parliament's legal protection that we need?

February 11, 1977
Canadian Human Rights Act
The purpose behind this bill is clear. It provides protection by giving effect to the following principles explicitly set out in clause 2 which reads:
Every individual should have an equal opportunity with other individuals to make for himself or herself the life that he or she is able and wishes to have, consistent with his or her duties and obligations as a member of society, without being hindered in or prevented from doing so by discriminatory practices-
Then, as well:
(b)	the privacy of individuals should be protected to the greatest extent consistent with public order and well-being.
These are principles which rest upon the inherent dignity and the equal and inalienable rights of all members of the human family. These are principles as fundamental as freedom itself. The freedoms for which liberal western societies strive are set out in well known landmark documents: the English Bill of Rights of 1689, the French Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen, the American Bill of Rights, and the Universal Declaration of the Rights of Man. Each of those statements was the result of historic struggles to defend dignity and freedom. Each of those statements sets forth the principles and standards by which all free societies stand ready to be judged. Those standards include equal entitlement to all rights and freedoms including equal opportunity for self-realization and the enjoyment of life. It may surprise hon. members to learn that at present there is no over-all protection of these freedoms at the federal level. There are no comprehensive guarantees against infringement within federal jurisdiction by corporations, citizens or government of many basic egalitarian rights Canadians should enjoy.
The Canadian Bill of Rights of 1960 provides principles for courts and officials to follow in interpreting federal laws. I pay tribute to a former prime minister, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) who passed the Canadian Bill of Rights which is now being given increasing force and effect by our courts. However, that law does not set standards for behaviour or impose any sanctions. Right now, a Pakistani who was refused service in a dining car on the CNR because the waiter disliked his looks would probably have no legal avenue of redress.
There is partial protection at the present time against discrimination in employment in that part of the private sector which is under federal jurisdiction. Part I of the Canada Labour Code, which deals with fair employment practices, applies to employment by organizations such as banks, railways and others under the jurisdiction of parliament. I pay tribute to the valuable work which successive ministers of labour and officials of the Department of Labour have done under the existing provisions of the Canada Labour Code.
However, that code does not include employment by the Crown in right of Canada. It does not cover these public servants in any way. Nor does it cover discrimination by age, sex, marital status or physical handicap. There is some protection against discrimination in government employment. As yet, however, there is no act of parliament which provides over-all, comprehensive prohibition of discriminatory conduct by offi-

cials and private individuals within the federal domain. These are significant lapses in the legal protection to which Canadians are entitled and which they deserve. These are significant gaps in the legal protection offered, for example, to the many women of Canada whose careers are seriously limited by sexism on the job, or to members of many minority groups for whom the relentless pressure of discrimination is too often a reality. In a free society like ours, in a multicultural and open society like ours, in a country made up of two founding peoples but which has also been built and peopled by those who have come from all over the world, and of all races and colours, to build their lives and their families, it is essential that we put into law and into practice within the federal jurisdiction a clear commitment to equality of opportunity and to protection from discrimination. The Canadian human rights bill is designed to provide that clear commitment and to provide, at long last, the comprehensive body of law now lacking at the federal level, a body of law to which all Canadians will be able to resort.
The anti-discrimination provisions of the bill declare the following to be prohibited grounds of discrimination: race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, age, sex, marital status, a conviction for which a pardon has been granted, and physical handicap for employment, where the handicap does not affect job performance. In choosing these grounds we have concentrated on major issues which have already been the subject of human rights legislation in Canada and the United States, on which a substantial body of law has emerged and upon which the proposed human rights commission can build. These prohibitions against discriminatory conduct will apply to all federal departments and agencies and any business or industry under federal jurisdiction.
As a further protection again racism, the bill contains a measure proscribing the dissemination of hate over the telephone. I think those of us who were here in parliament at the time, felt that we had dealt with this issue in the amendments to the Criminal Code which were passed relating to hate, but new practices have emerged. Under this bill the sending of repeated hate messages over federally-regulated telephones would be prohibited. The measure is more rigorous than section 281.2 of the Criminal Code, but it avoids-or I have endeavoured to draft it in such a way as to avoid-interference with legitimate expression of opinion.
These measures dealing with telephone hate messages are designed to provide an effective supplement to the provisions of the Criminal Code to combat the calculating traffickers in hate whose foul activities subvert the confidence of racial minorities in the protection that they are entitled to feel under the law. I might say in passing that the introduction of this bill seems to have attracted the attention of those hatemongers who use the telephone in this way, in that they have at least been diverted from the dirt they have disseminated about black people or people of the Jewish faith and have now instead directed their messages of hate to Roy McMurtry and myself-so at least we have provided protection for two minorities.
February 11, 1977

The bill also contains measures to combat sexism and sex role stereotyping at the workplace. About 30 recommendations of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women would be wholly or partially implemented or made easier to implement by the passage of this bill. Upon passage this will bring the number of status of women commission recommendations implemented, partially implemented or whose implementation has been facilitated to 103 of the 122 recommendations directed to the federal government in the commission's 1970 report.
Besides including grounds for discrimination such as sex and marital status which are not covered by the Canada Labour Code, the bill also requires that equal pay be given for work of equal value. This is the first time the language "work of equal value" has been used in Canadian law to express equal pay requirements. The Canada Labour Code, the earlier version of this bill and provincial statutes in this regard required only that equal pay be given for similar work. There was no consideration of value. In the course of the preparation of this bill and the consideration of the earlier one, I consulted with and listened to various women's rights organizations who are involved in this matter and who contend that under the previous formulation women employees could be hived off into low-paid "job ghettos" where they would never have a chance to do work similar to that of men. In these job ghettos women can be paid less even though the jobs are of equal value.
Let us consider, for example, a hypothetical trucking firm engaged in interprovincial or international activities. Perhaps all the women employees are office workers, while the male employees are dispatchers. Since these are similar jobs, equal pay would not be required under the old formulation. Under this bill, it will be possible to compare the effort, the skill, the responsibility and the conditions of work in the two jobs and to determine if they are of equal value. It is for this reason that the women's rights organizations wanted the equal value concept embodied in the law. That is why the International Labour Organization included this concept in its convention which Canada ratified in 1972. That is why I have included it for the first time in Canadian law through this bill.

speechtext:
I am sure that before this bill is passed we will be told by some that this concept of equal value will place an intolerable burden upon employers. I do not accept that and I would like to make it very clear right now, beyond any possibility of misunderstanding, that as a parliament we would be wrong to accept that the economy of this country can survive only on the basis of unequal pay for women doing work equal in value to that being done by men. Enforcement of these and other provisions will be carried out under the proposed legislation by a human rights commission. The commission will have wide powers, including the power to establish tribunals able to impose severe financial penalties.
Besides initiating and seeing to the investigation of complaints, the commission would be able to issue guidelines interpreting the application of the act. The commission as it gains experience will, I hope, under the provisions of the legislation consider and recommend to parliament that the prohibited grounds of discrimination be broadened or added to as circumstances warrant. As benefits a body one of whose tasks will be to sit in judgment on government conduct, the human rights commission because, for example, of all the provisions that relate to the federal public sector as well as the private public sector, would unlike those in some other jurisdictions, will be independent of government and responsible only to parliament.
In preparing the bill, I have noted the comments of people like Mr. Borovoy of the Canadian Civil Liberties Association who generally have supported the bill but who have made the valid comment that the real test of this legislation and of our commitment to act against discriminatory practices is whether the commission will have the personnel and the budget to carry out its mandate effectively. When the bill reaches committee we are going to examine the question of resources and a proposed budget. It has been planned, in conjunction with Treasury Board, to give the commission the personnel and resources to carry out its mandate. I agree with those who say that the question of resources is crucial to the real effectiveness of the commission and I am satisfied that what we will be proposing will meet with approval.
Turning to a different aspect of the bill, that is, part IV, Mr. Speaker, I noted in my introductory remarks that apart from the question of discrimination, the question of individual access to government records is not a uniquely Canadian issue. It is a problem faced by most highly developed societies. My officials and I have carefully studied the experience of these countries. We believe the provisions in the human rights bill provide the widest possible access and the firmest safeguards consistent with our parliamentary system and the interest of the public as a whole. I believe that the provisions of this bill, taken as a whole, will give Canadians more effective protection against administrative misuse of personal information in government files than that now enjoyed by citizens of the United States.

February 11, 1977
Canadian Human Rights Act
The United States privacy act and part IV of Bill C-25 have the same basic objectives. Both acts have basically the same approach to providing access through the creation of a federal index of personal information banks. Both acts provide for an individual to see his file and to propose changes if the individual feels that errors exist. Both acts provide for administration procedures to warn users of the file that the subject of the record objects to particular information in the record if an institution refuses to make corrections.
There are, however, certain differences which lead me to believe that the protection afforded under this bill of the rights to Canadians with respect to abuse of their personal information in government banks is effectively greater than the rights of Americans. Under the United States act, the non-elected head of any agency can decide whether an information bank is exempt from access. Under Bill C-25, it is not a bureaucrat but an elected minister who, in the case of a whole information bank, must first obtain the approval of the governor in council before any exemptions from access can be granted. Moreover, under the United States act there are certain blanket exemptions. An entire information bank can be exempted just because it belongs to the Central Intelligence Agency. In Canada, access to the data banks of the most sensitive agencies is not automatically excluded.
As a further safeguard against administrative or other abuse of personal information in government files, the bill requires that a member of the human rights commission be appointed privacy commissioner, with the power to review at public expense any complaint by any individual that he or she is being denied rights under this part of the act. Like the Auditor General or the Official Languages Commissioner, the privacy commissioner would be independent of the government and would report at least annually to parliament, and could include-and under the act is empowered to include-in his report accounts of individual cases where an error or injustice is not rectified. This approach is consistent with our parliamentary system of responsible government. It rests the ultimate responsibility for decisions concerning access to personal information upon the minister responsible to parliament. Establishing the office of privacy commissioner will make the government more accountable to parliament and, through parliament, to all Canadians.
I indicated at the beginning of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, that I share the frustration of those who are disappointed at this point that the bill has not yet been passed into law. We are now on second reading and I hope we will make good progress. There are members of this House who have deep knowledge of the matters raised in the bill and who will want to make a contribution to debate and to the committee proceedings. There are other groups in the community involved with this issue who I know, from correspondence and discussions with them, will want to make suggestions to the parliamentary committee for changes in the law. All of that is welcome and I hope we will be able to agree in a non-partisan way that this bill be passed by this House and the other place and made the law of the land by June 30 this year. I hope that those who

want to come to parliament and make suggestions about the bill will make them in a constructive, non-partisan way in order to help us reach that objective of enactment by June 30.
Nearly 30 years ago Canada and the other members of the United Nations approved the Universal Declaration of the Rights of man. About 17 years ago we passed the Canadian Bill of Rights. In the meantime, Canada has acceded to two further international instruments on the subject of human rights: the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. It is time we met the urgent need for a domestic charter against discrimination recognized by all as a commitment to building a nation in which denial of equal rights and opportunities is totally unacceptable.

Mr. Speaker, first may I thank the minister for the shortness of his speech. I am not sure whether I can be as brief. I have the problem, at twenty minutes to one, that unless I can finish in twenty minutes my train of thought might be interrupted. I do not think the minister need worry too much about his June 30 target. From the point of view of my party, I can tell the minister that we welcome the bill and will be anxious to see it progress as rapidly as possible, given the fact-as the minister himself said-that it is important that not only ministers but others speak to this bill at this stage. I do not see that there will be any disposition to hold it up, although there will be a disposition in committee to suggest and recommend, in the non-partisan way the minister asked for, some amendments that may improve the law. That is an undertaking which I gladly give on behalf of the party of which I am proud to be a part.
For many years I have been carrying around a little quotation. I think it puts the matter in perspective. The quotation is from a Russian emigre to Paris, a philosopher and theologian called Berdyaev. He said that the law may compel men to be just, but it cannot compel them to be brothers. Pity, mercy, love-these are works of grace in freedom and not works of a compelling law. 1 think the minister agrees with that sentiment. It is not enough, as the minister admits by introducing this bill, to have before us such injunctions from splendid philosophers. There is a duty on us, as legislators, to put in place a code or frame of reference which would allow those elements which philosophers want to be part of our citizenship to come into play.
I was not in this House when the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) introduced the Bill of Rights. The common law lawyers of this country universally condemned that concept-and I am not being partisan; I am trying to put this question in its historical perspective. The common law lawyers said that the bill was an unnecessary frill in our jurisprudence. I remember my own misgivings, I having been brought up in that tradition which was concerned about
February 11, 1977

these things being set down in statute form. Yet, as the minister says, not all in this country are of the common law tradition. We are of many traditions, and it is important to have the human rights commission in place and to have the Bill of Rights. I hope to serve here long enough to see us enshrine the Bill of Rights as an inviolate part of our constitutional arrangements when we patriate the constitution.

speechtext:
The minister may remember that the common law lawyers objected to the Bill of Rights. There was some debate about it. I will not comment on how the Bill of Rights has been used over the years. I happen to think it has been a useful code for those who otherwise might have strayed, and my remarks apply to those acting within the jurisdiction of the government of Canada.
I also happen to think that we have very few commonly shared heritages. Obviously, a Bill of Rights of some 17 years standing and a flag adopted in 1965, I think, are not yet enshrined in the minds of all Canadians as part of their shared heritage; but they will be, I am sure. Similarly, I hope that the proposed human rights commission, the establishment of which, after all, follows that of the ten human rights commissions now in place in the provinces, will give Canadians the feeling that in this land they can move about and participate without fear of discrimination.
It is curious that within five days of ten years ago, on February 16, 1967, the government established the Royal Commission on the Status of Women. Three and a half years later, on September 28, 1970, the commission tabled its report and recommendations, including the establishment of a human rights commission. In July, 1975, the then minister of justice introduced Bill C-72. In November, 1976, the present bill was introduced. Perhaps it will interest those who read the reports of our debates to know that I was fascinated, as a member of parliament, to watch the by-play-that may not be an accurate description-to watch the nervousness among members of the public service with regard to the privacy part of the bill.
I was privy to one or two secrets, if I may say so. You cannot live in this community without at some time rubbing shoulders with some of the first-rate public servants who serve our country. I know that the privacy provisions of the bill underwent at least 15 drafts. I do not think there were any cardiac arrests during that period, but there were some pretty nervous people in the public service who thought that at last the government was going to bell the sacred cow of secrecy. That will not come about; it is not part of the bill. I think the Canadian Bar Association told the minister what has to be done in the area of secrecy. Nevertheless, it is amusing and somewhat worrying to note that many who serve the country in the public service are worried about information being freely available.
As I have said, the present bill was introduced in November, 1976. It has two main purposes. The intention is, first, to prohibit discrimination on certain grounds within federal jurisdiction; second, to establish certain measures to protect the
Canadian Human Rights Act
privacy of individuals. I hope hon. member will not mind if I quote a paragraph or two from the 1970 recommendations of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women. At page 65 of the report the commission recommended:
-that (a) federal... human rights commission be set up that would
(a)	be directly responsible to parliament-
The minister proposes to do this. I continue quoting:
(b)	have power to investigate the administration of human rights legislation as well as the power to enforce the law by laying charges and prosecuting offenders;
(c)	include within the organization for a period of seven to ten years, a division dealing specifically with the protection of women's rights; and
(d)	suggest changes in human rights legislation and promote widespread respect for human rights.
Presumably, once the commission has been set up that last recommendation will be included in its ongoing obligations. I listened carefully to what the minister said. Fie suggested that the Advisory Council on the Status of Women during the years since 1970 has been commenting, urging and recommending. I think this is the appropriate time to compliment it on its restlessness about this legislation. The council has been positive in its views. As far as I can tell, it has been quite non-discriminating-if I can use that word-about its requests. It has been free to come and give recommendations to opposition party spokesmen, and so on. I agree with the minister that although the bill in its present form may not meet all the council's urgings, at least the legislation has been launched. In 1975 the Advisory Council on the Status of Women made a statement which recognized:
-the crucial need for federal involvement in the human rights area, not only from the point of view of the status of women but in the context of the increased racial and other tensions manifest in our society-
It recommended the immediate tabling of the human rights legislation, and here we are at last. I am sorry to note that one part of the advisory council's statement is brutally, demeaningly true, sorry that there is indeed an increase in racial and other tensions manifest in our country. We will not serve our constituents or our country if we fail to recognize this fact. It is not only confined to one or two of the great metropolitan areas. I think of the evil jokes spread across the country. Perhaps somebody has done a study.
It seems to me that if you could trace the racial joke or the ethnic joke, it would follow the waves of the settlement of this country. In other words, historians could pick out the jokes which were told about one minority 100 years ago and find them recurring as the waves of immigration took place. To put it in another way, the Newfoundlander today is all too often the recipient of the same type of demeaning comment as the Polish Canadian would have been 50 years ago, and presumably the Irish Canadian 100 years ago. Perhaps somebody has done a study on those lines. I am not a behavioural scientist, but I know that this form of humour is still very demeaning to the part of our society which is the butt of these jokes.
The minister was right when he spoke of the use of the telephone. It is curious that these bullying cowards do these things using our technology. They paint out the signs at night.

February 11, 1977
Canadian Human Rights Act
Nobody would paint out a bilingual sign in the daytime. Few people would dare to perpetrate the type of language they use on the telephone if they had to do it face to face. But unsigned letters come to all of us and, of course, the telephone is used for the same type of thing. Unhappily, there are some who, because of the length of time during which they have been in the country or the disability from which they might suffer or, if I can put it this way without being arrogant, from a lack of serenity or assurance with regard to their acceptance in society, are put off by this type of thing. It is unfortunate, in my view, but legislation is the only solution if it is to be stopped.
I was curious to Find a reference to a friend of the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Sharp). I am sure the hon. member for Eglinton knows the works of Thomas Carlyle. Carlyle said we have no duty of tolerance to the intolerant. At one stage of my life I would have been overcome by a statement like that, but I do not think Carlyle was right. It was very nice in the leather-bound books of the day, but we cannot be satisfied with that type of aphorism. We have to be intolerant and that is why in the ultimate resort the technology of the telephone hate campaign has to be interrupted by a statute. It will not end it, but it will be evidence in the statute books of the country.
Really, what the government is attempting in the human rights legislation might be likened to lighting a candle toward respect for each and every human being. I suggest that the cultivation of such respect requires more than law. It requires a fundamental commitment to the worth of human kind. I do not mean to preach, but it occurs to me that to respect, you have to work at it. It is often not easy for those of us who are democrats to respect everybody at all times. It requires a fundamental commitment on our part. I am not sure, but I suspect that respect for one's brother is not innate in our psyche; it has to be nurtured and worked on. Surely the minister and others who will be participating in this debate and who are committed to human rights would agree that a wound to my brother wounds me, and that the outrage in the subway, whether it is to somebody in Toronto, Vancouver or Fundy-Royal-because none of us is immune-is wounding ourselves.
I have been fascinated by the phenomenon in the United States of the television program "Roots" which was seen by more Americans than any other program since the invention of that technology. There was an example of a group of American citizens for whom a large part of their history was unknown. The fact that the program took a family through from its origins in West Africa until the present day must have been compelling for both black and white Americans.
Lastly, on this point, because it is about one o'clock, I might say that the small "1" liberal "schtick" of inviting a black to break bread with you might not work out the way you expect it to. He may not share one's own aspirations with regard to material things, for instance. Jules Feiffer pointed this out in a powerful cartoon. The answer is, if you ask one black to lunch, ask two in case it doesn't work out.

May I call it one o'clock?
At one o'clock the House took recess.

Mr. Speaker, I did complain about having my speech interrupted by the lunch hour, but I find now I have to withdraw a couple of things. One is my complaint about that. Then to my horror I find I was much too tough on Thomas Carlyle. In any race for immortality between myself and Thomas Carlyle, Carlyle would obviously win, and he has done so again. What I was trying to say was that we could not be tolerant of intolerance. I have had discussions with certain people who find that even with the most liberal editing they could not make head nor tail of my attempt to savage poor Carlyle, so the only thing to do is what the lawyers call confession and avoidance. I make it clear that the hon. member for Eglinton is not a contemporary of Thomas Carlyle.
In getting some thoughts together for this speech today, I came across another curious paradox. It has to do with Eldridge Cleaver who ten years ago was sought in the capitals of America and the world as being an outrageous radical, as undoubtedly I think he was. Among other things, Eldridge Cleaver went to Cuba and found his radicalism tested there because the generals in Cuba are white and the foot soldiers black; at least, that is what he said. So a lot of things happened even in American society to tell people that discrimination has no boundaries in the world, and no matter what the ideology, discrimination and racism can creep in. To Cleaver's credit, in this regard in any event, he saw the error of earlier days.
Another paradox I want to cite is a peculiarly Canadian phenomenon. I refer to people who sing brotherhood songs at service clubs on Monday and then busily go to private clubs which discriminate on the basis of colour, creed, and so on, on Tuesday. This is in no way an indictment of the service clubs, because I think they have contributed immeasurably to Canada. But in 1977 there is, surely, no place for any club, private or otherwise, the membership of which is affected by racial origin, colour or what have you. I must say that there is a high degree of hypocrisy in this aspect of our contemporary life. I assume that discrimination and prejudice have their origins in fear and threat, a threat to what people think of as their own little piece of earth, because there can be no other basis,on which such cruelty is founded. I should like to end the philosophical part of these few remarks with the thought that one definition of "man" surely is that he is a hoping creature. Once man gives up hope, he gives up everything. Hope is an essential condition of our very humanity.
I should like to compliment the minister and others who have had a part to play in this bill. The bill is an expression, in legislative form, of the hope that we have that practices that are outlawed will end some day in Canada. The greatest hope
February 11, 1977

we could have, of course, is that the commissioners themselves could, in that utopian day, work themselves out of a job. I do not believe that would ever happen, but it would be the ultimate of man's feelings about man.
As I said earlier, there are human rights commissions now in place in all ten of the provinces. This bill will apply to the federal jurisdiction and also to the Yukon and Northwest Territories. The minister was quick to confess that it will not in itself end discrimination. There is a fascinating book on the whole subject of discrimination and prejudice written by an expert, Gordon W. Allport, entitled "The Nature of Prejudice". He writes:
Legislation, if enforced, may be a sharp tool in the battle against discrimination. Legal action, however, has only an indirect bearing on the reduction of personal prejudice. It cannot coerce thoughts or instill subjective tolerance. Law is meant to control the outward expression of intolerance. But outward expression, psychology knows, has an eventual effect on inner habits of thought and feeling. For this reason legislative action can be listed as one of the major methods of reducing, not only public discrimination, but private prejudice as well.
In a way, that is what I was trying to say this morning about the Bill of Rights, that its eventual effect on people will be that they know that they and others have rights, and the eventual effect on people in the human rights field will be the same.
There are, of course, some criticisms. Because the House has been rather generous to me about time, I will not go through all of them. I will save that part for the committee stage. Here I want to say how helpful the Canadian Association of University Teachers have been. They think that political views, family relationships and sexual orientation should be included as grounds. They are also concerned about physical handicaps, the restrictive way in which the legislation is now drafted. They feel that the matters related to employment, that is the phrase in the statute, appear to exclude the physically handicapped from the protection of clauses 5 and 6.
There was another very interesting comment. I heard it spontaneously. I think another member will be raising it later, so I just note it in passing. Most of the comments about age are with regard to pension and retirement. Actually, age is a prohibited ground of discrimination. Clause 7 states that employment cannot be denied on the ground of age, but clause 14 refers to normal age of retirement. Therefore, it would not be illegal to fire an employee because he has reached retirement age. In committee we will have to consider whether the bill condones systematic discrimination in the form of compulsory retirement, or possibly even a statement from the minister at the committee stage will suffice.
Others have commented, including the Advisory Council on the Status of Women, that there is not sufficient protection in this bill for the handicapped in matters other than employment. The minister spent a good deal of time on the new phraseology "work of equal value". I was particularly interested in what he had to say. We have to confess that many employers have taken advantage of this sort of grouping throughout the years. Presumably the hon. member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson), who will be speaking, will address herself to
Canadian Human Rights Act
this matter. We have had some very interesting conversations with people who have reflected on this aspect, including the Ontario ministry of labour which put out a pamphlet in October of last year entitled "Equal Pay for Work of Equal Value". They discuss some of the dilemmas. Again, I am not going to read into the record that long discussion. However, the House should be reminded of some of the difficulties.
To the extent that formal processes for comparison of jobs would be required by government, rather than merely encouraged or assisted, equal pay for work of equal value would carry with it a presumption of increased intervention by government in the collective bargaining and wage determination process. The question arises whether this is desirable or acceptable. Reactions to the federal government's heightened role in this area since the anti-inflation controls took effect in October, 1975, suggests that no consensus presently exists on the question. Despite the minister's comment about it, I hope that perhaps from this debate and what other people will say some of the dilemmas can be laid to rest.
Countries such as Belgium, Luxembourg, Ireland, West Germany, Denmark, France, the United Kingdom, Italy and The Netherlands have also attempted to deal with the removal of sex discriminatory pay situations and have generally accepted the principle that pay rates be established using a single set of criteria for both sexes. However, there seems to be quite widespread recognition that progress toward equal pay for work of equal value has been slow. Just because I make this gloomy comment- it is actually a gloomy comment from the Ontario government's paper-does not mean that my party or anyone else who has thought about this matter does not support what the minister is trying to say. Perhaps I had better withdraw those comments. I would expect that a large part of the work of the new commission will be trying to make this part of the law applied fairly.
There are one or two further comments I would like to make. In clause 12 there is another definition of a discriminatory practice. The Advisory Council on the Status of Women feels that this clause is far too limited because it applies only to published notices and signs. The advisory council feels that advertising in other media should not be overlooked. The clause does not seem to attack the problem of, for example, stereotypes that are rampant in the advertising world about women.
Others in my party, particularly the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), will be dealing carefully and thoroughly with what I might call the second part of the bill dealing with privacy. I think it is fair to make this comment, and I do it without any particular partisan feeling. Had this bill been part of the law of Canada, the type of activity that we witnessed in the last couple of weeks, the so-called blacklist, would in itself have been an infraction. If not, then this law is not very effective.

Well, I wanted something better than "petard". I am hoist with my own cliche, really. However, the government seems to be nervous about risks. It takes risks once in a while by funding organizations and then seems surprised that some of the people who attend conferences say things the government does not particularly like to hear. This becomes elevated into some sort of a documental state warning the ministry that so-and-so may eventually bring about the downfall of western democracy. I have never been as nervous about western democracy or about the Canadian government as this government seems to be, and I hope that in future this type of thing can be stopped where it should be, in the hands of the minister-I suspect that it will be, and I mean this as a compliment to the new minister-or else that public servants will have a right to deal with it under the legislation.
The House has been very indulgent. When I started I said to the minister that this party understands the timetable. It has been ten years almost to the day since the royal commission was established. The bill has been drifting around Ottawa for some time in one form or another, and although other people will want to make their contributions the bill will be supported by this party at second reading. However, we will be expecting, particularly on the privacy part of the bill, substantial amendments at the committee stage. But neither the minister nor the government need have any doubt about the feelings of the Progressive Conservative party about the need for Canada to fall in line with the provinces with regard to having human rights legislation.
One last thing: the fact is often overlooked that sometimes we can do things in this country rather well. One place where some things are done very well is the province of Ontario, where the human rights commission and the operation of the act are among the best in North America. I hope nobody runs for cover or gets out a red covered partisan manual refuting

that. In other parts of the world Ontario is looked upon as a bellwether in the human rights field. I hope that this government, being the national government, can supplant in excellence what Ontario has been able to do.
Just a few moments ago I had a discussion with the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). He may be wanting to speak, but he said something very wise and it provides me with a neat ending. He said he hoped that most of the work-and I am paraphrasing him-of the commission will be in conciliation and not in prosecution. I believe very deeply that the fewer prosecutions and the more conciliation, the better it will be for the human rights commission, because that will mean that slowly there shall be public acceptance for the concept.

However, we are certainly not going to be in any sense responsible for its not passing quickly. There are matters which have to be examined thoroughly. This is a very important bill and we propose to do our duty, but we think that can be done without taking a great deal of time in this case. Those parts of the present bill which proscribe discrimination have been supported by this party for a long time and we will continue to support that principle by voting in support of the bill at second reading.
Those kind remarks in no way refer to part IV of the bill which is entitled "protection of personal information". We regard that part of the bill as being a farce and we think that the Canadian Bar Association rightly described it as totally inadequate. I shall deal further with that matter later. There are some matters which will have to be discussed in committee, of course, but there is no purpose in holding up second reading by dealing with any of those details.

We certainly approve extending the prohibitions against discrimination to discrimination on the grounds of age, sex, marital status or physical handicaps. To us, this bill-which might have been produced before now-is timely because it is obvious that there is a serious danger of the poison of racial feelings being expressed in a way which is entirely damaging and harmful to our community. Most of us who have been around a little while can recall the immense burden of human suffering which was caused by racial discrimination flowing from so-called racial superiority, and we certainly support provisions to prohibit the various forms of discrimination which are mentioned.
I would also like to join with the hon. member for Fundy-Royal in commending the excellent contribution made in this field by the Royal Commission on the Status of Women, which made recommendations along these lines in 1970, for the persistence with which it has carried them out. I commend that because I think it is important to know that although things in this parliament sometimes go slowly, if people are persistent in good causes they can sometimes get results. This is a cheering illustration of a case where results have followed a very persistent, informed and reasonable presentation of a case.
I single out the women's movements of this country, and the special committees upon which they have worked, for special notice because I think they deserve it. Even at this hour I have a copy of background notes on this bill which were prepared for the Advisory Council on the Status of Women and only made available in January of 1977. I hope that the committee, when it gets the bill, will have, not a vast number of witnesses, because that would delay the matter, but some experienced witnesses to deal with the act who will make their suggestions and give us their advice.
A problem is raised on the question of retirement. The phrase used is that there shall be no discrimination in regard to age, or the normal age of retirement, in dealing with that type of discrimination, but my recollection is that that is not well defined and is left to the impersonal operations of the market. So that if it becomes customary in some industries to retire people at the age of 30 or 40, then presumably the bill has no application. I think that should be looked into very carefully.
There is another factor which we think should be looked into very carefully. That is, as has been mentioned already by the hon. member for Fundy-Royal, that-as I think is the case in nearly all the provincial acts dealing with this subject matter-stress should be laid on a process of conciliation. It is all very well to have sanctions and prosecutions in the courts, but I am not at all satisfied that the courts, which sometimes lack experience in this type of matter, are necessarily the best instruments in which to seek enforcement of the bill. They may have their part to play, but there is a process of conciliation, a process for seeking to get a change of mind, an attitude as well as merely formal compliance with the act. We think the bill
Canadian Human Rights Act
requires to be carefully looked at to see whether adequate machinery is provided encouraging that type of conciliation which has been proven useful in other jurisdictions.
There is an exception which we think is dangerous; that is the one which exempts action which can be described as a bona fide occupational requirement. There is no definition of this so-called bona fide occupational requirement, and we are fearful that that expression might well be used as a loophole through which some people can escape from complying with or obeying the spirit of the legislation. We know that in England the sex discrimination act, dealing with a similar matter, clearly defines what is meant by a bona fide occupational requirement, and we think it is necessary to put that in this bill.
Now I want to deal with part IV of the bill which is called "protection of personal information". In our view, as I have mentioned already, this is utterly inadequate. I think it is a good example of what good legislation should not be. The minister, in the usual fulsome way in which he refers to his own proposals, has described this part of the bill dealing with personal information as an improvement on previous legislation and as establishing a legislative framework for protecting the individual right of access to personal information.
We do not see it in that way. Part IV is full of exemptions and exceptions that are so sweeping that in all likelihood, even if they had any virtue to begin with, they would turn out to be unworkable because they are so broad. The exemptions are all in the hands of the minister who is declared to be the appropriate minister to deal with this act. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) has even suggested that somehow or other this part of the act would take the place of a freedom of information bill such as exists in the United States and some European countries.

This suggestion-I thought I heard him make it, and certainly the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is reported as having made it in discussing the freedom of information bill-is a total misconception. The committee on regulations and other statutory instruments, as the Minister of Justice knows very well, has been struggling with the freedom of information bill. The committee travelled to the United States and some of its members travelled to Europe. We have spent a great deal of time on it. I am sure that if he had thought for one moment it was worthwhile consulting that committee, he would have been told that there is no relevance in the statute we are dealing with now to a proper freedom of information bill.

We were impressed, and I think that is true of all members of the committee, with the practicality, the clear, forthright and, indeed, successful manner in which the freedom of information act is administered in the United States. But I ask hon. members to take a look at part IV of the bill and note some of the exemptions. I will not attempt to go into all of them. Practically the whole part consists of exemptions. The bill deals only with federal information banks which are defined in the definitions section. It entitles an individual to see the records in these federal information banks. But the appropriate minister may, with the approval of the governor in council, exempt or restrict the information when he determines that it might be injurious to international relations, national defence or security, federal-provincial relations, or when it is likely to disclose information obtained or prepared by the government or any part of the government in relation to national security, detection or prevention of crime generally, or in the course of the investigation of offences against any act of parliament. So if in the course of investigation they collect any information of an alleged infringement of any act of parliament, the information can be exempted.
The minister also may exempt all material detailed by him to be detrimental to the custody, control or supervision of any person under sentence. That is another fairly large exemption. Further, the appropriate minister can prevent the disclosure of information which is described as confidential to the Queen's Privy Council of Canada, or any information relating to investigations pertaining to the enforcement or administration of any act of parliament.
Anything we investigate that is related to the administration of parliament can be exempted, or which might reveal personal information concerning any individual, or any information that impedes the functioning of a court of law or other tribunal, or which might disclose legal opinions or advice provided to a government institution. Mr. Speaker, since when have legal opinions become sacrosanct? I know the rules of confidentiality-that is, the confidence of the client-but this is a sort of general theory. The Minister of Justice knows about this because a parliamentary committee was refused permission to find out what was the basis of information being handed out wholesale by his department. A blanket of secrecy is put down by the minister himself on the efforts of members of parliament to find out what is being done in government. This provision is on a par with that. I think it is time we got rid of the myth that just by putting something in a legal opinion it is exempt from disclosure.
There is an even stranger provision. If, in the opinion of the minister, the harm of the disclosure would outweigh the benefit, then it could be made exempt. This bill says, in effect- and I put it in general phraseology-that anything the minister thinks should be disclosed, can be disclosed, and if there is anything the minister thinks should not be disclosed, it will be exempt. From the way some of the ministries have been behaving, I am quite sure much material would be exempt.

In our view, the act is a perpetuation of the reliance of the government on secrecy and its determination that we should not have an open system of government. By putting forward a measure that on its face requires something to be disclosed, and then it is eaten away by exemptions, makes the measure meaningless in practice. This is the government's method of holding on to the pattern of secrecy which characterizes its attitude in these matters.
The freedom of information act in the United States may not be perfect, but I think it has made useful and valuable changes in their law. This is not a light issue, Mr. Speaker. There are no doubt many reasons why the people of Canada and this parliament should not have confidence in the government. To me it is clear that this practice of general secrecy is a good enough reason for the people of Canada to get rid of this government as soon as possible. We are tired of a method of operation which conceals from the people of Canada and the parliament of Canada what the government is doing about various things.
Part IV of this bill is an illustration of how they seem to think we are eternally gullible enough to thank the great government for saying, "You can look up a freedom of information bank if you do not fall within some of the wide exemptions that are illustrated." An open society is important because you cannot have a participatory democracy-in which this government believes in theory-without information. To pretend that part IV of the bill is a real step forward toward making information available to people is a farce. In committee we shall do whatever is appropriate to have this clause removed from a bill which is certainly valuable in other parts which deal with discrimination. In its so-called protection of information it is a worthless piece of paper.

The bill before us today is, indeed, as the minister has said, a greatly improved version of the human rights bill, Bill C-72 which was before us in the last session, and to me one of the most significant improvements is that this bill establishes the principle of equal pay for work of equal value. The average female worker in Canada earns 40 per cent to 45 per cent less than the average male worker, and the gap between the two is widening. This massive earnings differential is due in part to the evident failure of our present equal pay legislation. It also results from the fact that women tend to be segregated in lower paying jobs-particularly in secretarial, clerical and service work.
Contrary to public opinion, this occupational segregation of women has increased during the past decade. "Equal pay for equal work" legislation which has been in force in Canada for over two decades compares the rate of pay of women and men in the same establishment on the basis of the same or similar work. In practice, however, comparison of similar jobs has often been avoided. Different job titles, or slight differences in work schedules enable, for example, a male janitor to earn more than a female cleaner. The argument has been made that employers undervalue women's work simply because jobs are staffed by women.
It can also be shown that when men and women perform jobs requiring comparable levels of skill, education and responsibility, men are usually better paid. This discrimination often comes as a great surprise to fair-minded men. A friend of mine who, in his own university, had studied the jobs, pay and skills of men and women on the non-academic staff, confidently expecting he would find no inequity because his university was progressive and followed good personnel practices, found to his great surprise that women in administrative support jobs by and large had two years more formal education than men and were paid about $1,000 a year less. He also found, as one might expect, that the title of the job was different, depending on whether it was performed by a man or a woman. These kinds of inequities, hopefully, will be dealt with by using the concept of "equal remuneration for work of equal value", rather than that of "equal pay for equal work".
The notion of "equal pay for work of equal value" allows for the comparison of unlike jobs, or of jobs that are not precisely the same on the basis of objective criteria of skill, effort, responsibility and conditions of work. We are not talking, in the bill before us, of a massive intervention in the marketplace. We are talking about guidelines for agencies, whether they be government departments or Crown agencies, which already have fairly sophisticated personnel departments, job evaluations and descriptions. Really, it is a matter of doing this differently and perhaps weighing some factors differently.
Canadian Human Rights Act
Men as well as women should benefit in the long term from an equal pay amendment. A gradual elimination of sex role stereotypes linked to occupations offers more possibilities for both men and women to make vocational choices based on their own talents and skills, as opposed to choices which are limited by stereotyped expectations. Once experience has been gained in applying this kind of legislation, it should be possible to develop a body of expertise in its application.
In 1972, the government of Canada, with the concurrence of provincial governments, ratified the 1951 International Labour Convention No. 100 which was concerned with the principle of "equal remuneration for work of equal value". In his announcement, the then minister of labour stated that "the basic obligation of a ratifying country is the pursuit of policies aimed at the achievement of the objectives stated in the convention". A number of years have gone by during which the implementation of this basic obligation has been studied. I have been interested to note, at meetings of the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration, that officials have gradually changed their initial position, of thinking that there was no way in which this idea could be implemented, to one of finding that the idea had possibilities.
I note, with interest, that the commission is to be empowered, among other things, to play a role in public education and research. I should like to see this idea applied narrowly and immediately in the development of mechanisms which will ensure compliance with the intent of this legislation, particularly in the public service. Unfortunately, a number of blocks to the advancement of women exist not because of bad intent but because old rigidities have not been modernized. This applies, for example, to job qualifications. Until recently, one of the qualifications for investigative jobs with the ministry of consumer and corporate affairs was five years' police experience. That was the qualification needed for the investigation of misleading advertising practices. Since few women in Canada have experience in a police force, the effect of that requirement was to introduce a male-oriented bias to selection. Obviously, for this kind of job some experience in investigative techniques is necessary. Surely, however, with careful selection of people and adequate in-service training it should be possible to find some equivalencies which would not have the effect of excluding women.
Similarly, until recently there was an absolute requirement of experience in labour administration for many jobs in the Department of Labour, experience which up to this point in our lives has not been generally available to women. Again, one finds few or no women at all in some of these positions. Given an intelligent assessment of equivalencies and an insistence on in-service staff training, it should be possible, surely, to include some women in such jobs. It has been the experience of those who have worked in large organizations, whether in the public service or in the private sector, that good staff do not fall like manna from heaven. They are generally the logical product of intelligent staff development and in-service training.
