Another program which was designed to find "promotable people" and develop their careers, but is not doing this for women, is the data stream system. Again, certain rigidities have crept in here. The "buzz" words which describe the needed qualifications tend to exclude women. For example, a master's degree in business administration tends to be much more highly regarded than perhaps a master's in social work or in nursing. Actually, the latter kind of specialization has often been seen as a handicap. Surely this is not reasonable, because although for certain types of jobs financial and business expertise are essential, there is more than one kind of administration. One thinks of an administrator as somebody who can create a climate in which people can work to capacity and as somebody who knows how to enable people to work effectively. The application of interpersonal skills in a task-oriented way is not necessarily something for which the M.B.A. is the only possible kind of preparation.
I hope that with the introduction of this new legislation and the requirement that equal pay be given for work of equal value we shall also find attention given to some of these mechanisms which will reduce the rigidity.
Another important element in this legislation is the inclusion of unions. The record of the unions in promoting the status of women has not been impressive. Flowever, some very encouraging resolutions were passed at the last annual meeting of the Canadian Labour Council and one must hope that this represents a change of heart, one which I am sure will be helped by the existence of the legislation before us.
When I was in Washington last September I met with an American unionist who told me that some of her associates had successfully sued her union for a large amount of money on the grounds of inadequate representation. Her comment was that the result had been to create in that union and in others a greater sensitivity to the needs of women members. But she added; "I really hate to see our union hit with a great big fine because, after all, it is our own money." I agree that union funds could probably be used for many more constructive purposes than the payment of legal fees and I would hope that the existence of the law, together with changing social attitudes, will result in more effective representation by the unions of the needs of their women members.
The fact that the commission has been created with a considerable degree of independence, and that it is to report directly to parliament, is important precisely because the commission has the power to review and comment on federal rules, orders and the like, and if these are found to be inconsistent with the principles set out in the bill, to include such matters in the report to parliament. This aspect of the commission's work will be extremely significant because the barriers to the advancement of women in the public service and in Crown corporations are often constituted less by overt prejudice and deliberate exclusionary tactics than by rigidities in old-fashioned hiring practices.

Two major criticisms of the bill have come to my attention through the mail and also by telephone. The first is that it places too much emphasis on negotiation, that it "lacks teeth", that it does not go quickly enough to court action. The other side of that criticism I heard, in Washington, in September when women in the women's rights movement were talking about big settlements which one corporation or another had been obliged to make as a result of a decision under the equal rights legislation. They told me that these court actions dragged on for so long, and large corporations were so well able to wait matters out, that the individuals concerned rarely benefited. One disheartened person said to me that perhaps equal rights legislation should have been called the "lawyers and economists social security act".
The emphasis on negotiation in this Bill and on attempts to reach a settlement before resorting to punitive action is one which fits the Canadian situation better. I think we have more taste and talent for negotiation and trying to reason matters out than for engaging in fierce fights. Moreover, we are smaller. We are dealing with organizations which are less entrenched. By and large we are dealing with situations where there is good will rather than otherwise, and I think that to use the heavy hand prematurely would probably not be in our interests. Nevertheless, it is well to have it in reserve, and I like the balance of the bill in that regard.
Turning to the second criticism, there are some who feel that questions having to do with employment should still be under the Canada Labour Code, that we are dealing here with a commercial transaction between a woman and an employer and that one ought not to be obliged to go to a human rights commission to get what is a basic right of that kind. I feel that this objection is met in the bill before us in several ways. First, there is the possibility of group action. A woman does not have to complain on her own; her union or group can lodge a complaint on her behalf. In the second place, there is the commission's power to initiate and examine. Then there is the fact that the inspection right under the Canadian Labour Code is retained. Inspectors in the Department of Labour retain the obligation to look for inequalities in pay. The accumulated expertise in the Department of Labour is retained and made use of.
I am sure that as with any bill some improvements will be made in committee, but I believe we are starting off with a bill which has many good features in it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on Bill C-25 which is an act to extend the present laws of Canada which proscribe discrimination and protect the rights of individuals.
I believe the Canadian people should know exactly what we are establishing here. This is a bill to provide for a Canadian human rights commission, and the powers and functions of the commission are described. It is provided, for instance, that full-time members of the commission are persons deemed to be employed in the Public Service of Canada for the purpose of the Public Service Superannuation Act and for the purpose of the Government Employees Compensation Act and any regulations under section 7 of the Aeronautics Act. Also the commission is to provide for the payment of witnesses' fees to persons appearing before tribunals, and a tribunal may award compensation in the manner prescribed to a victim of a discriminatory practice.
I am not a supporter of establishing another government department or of expanding the bureaucracy, but certainly 1 support the establishment of the human rights commission. I want to read into the record this afternoon some of the reasons why we need such a commission and also to relate some of the discriminatory ways in which some employees are being treated by Crown corporations.
The enforcement of human rights legislation has always been weak and difficult. The Canadian human rights commission will have the exclusive power to turn away a complainant if it thinks the problem can be solved elsewhere. It could shortly become the last resort for a complainant as a result of overwork. The individual may be forced to turn to other agencies or even the courts.
The cases I am going to discuss this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, are cases that have gone to the court but the individuals have still not been informed why they were dismissed by the Crown corporation concerned. The individual or group has no right of appeal should the commission refuse to take a complaint or decide it is without basis. Nowhere in this provision does it state that the complainant has the right to information collected by the commission during the course of the investigation. The enforcement of a person's human rights is entirely in the hands of the human rights commission. I think there should be some check on what they do or refuse to do, and I hope this aspect will be thoroughly discussed at the committee stage.
In terms of enforcement, the commission has no powers. It can at any stage after the filing of a complaint appoint a tribunal which will hold meetings to determine whether the act has been breached. If so, it issues binding orders which are enforceable in the same manner as an order of the Federal
Canadian Human Rights Act
Court of Canada. It will take at least two years or more before this commission is established. One wonders whether the new federal ombudsman will have problems with the bureaucracy in terms of their resenting an outsider's authority to poke into their procedures.
I have received a letter from the Canadian Telecommunications Division of the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway, Transport and General Workers. They have taken up the plight of one of their colleagues who has been dismissed by CN Telecommunications. The union has done everything it possibly can to find out why this person was dismissed, and the matter has been to the courts. Unbelievably, Mr. Speaker, even after going through the courts the courts did not demand that CN Telecommunications give a clear cut explanation of why this individual was dismissed. I should like to read the contents of this letter into the record.
On July 7/75 an employee of Canadian National Telecommunications in Whitehorse, Yukon Territory, named Bernie Maguire was called into the office of the Superintendent and was handed a letter which read:
"We regret to advise that subsequent to your being accepted for technical employment it has been determined that you do not fully meet entrance qualifications for such employment with our company. In view of this we must terminate your services immediately."
Mr. Maguire had been employed for eighteen months as a technician in the testing and regulating department and he was not allowed to return to his shift but was paid two weeks wages in lieu of notice.
The company refused to give Bernie any specific reason for being fired. He had passed both the company technical examinations and the company medical. He completed the probationary period which is six months, and his immediate supervisor, Mr. Bruce Lodge, stated that he was quite happy with Bernie's work. Bernie Maguire to this day has not been given the specific reason for his dismissal.
It was not until the case was heard by an arbitrator that the company finally offered a partial explanation. Bernie Maguire had failed to pass a security clearance.
It should be pointed out at this point that prior to his service with CN Telecommunications, Mr. Maguire served in the Canadian Army in the "cryptology" department and he was security cleared to a very high level.
So the House can see that this is a strange case. This man could not pass the security test of CN Telecommunications, but he was not considered a security risk for the army, which had a higher priority over CN Telecommunications. Continuing with the letter:
The case was grieved by the union representing Mr. Maguire, which is the Canadian Telecommunications Division of the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway, Transport and General Workers. It was grieved on the grounds that the collective agreement was violated and that an employee must be given a specific, valid reason for being dismissed. The case went through the first three stages of the grievance procedure with negative results. During this time MP John Reynolds brought the matter before the House of Commons and certain members and ministers promised support should the grievance procedure fail to bring satisfactory results, among them the Hon. Jean Marchand, hon. Ed Broadbent and hon. Erik Nielsen.
The case was heard by an arbitration board headed by Justice J. C. Anderson on November 14, 1975. The company stated that due to a contract with the Department of Supply and Services for the provision of communications facilities for the Canadian Police Information Circuit, all employees concerned must be security cleared.
In his decision Judge Anderson declared that the company had the right to set security as a standard of employment and that they were right in terminating the employment of Mr. Maguire. He ruled also that the company "could only do so upon paying the employee in lieu of reasonable notice, a sum of money at the rate of pay he was receiving at the time of his termination, equal to seventeen

February 11, 1977
Canadian Human Rights Act
(17) weeks of pay." He did not rule that Mr. Maguire should be told the specific reason for his dismissal.
I am going to give the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) a copy of this letter and I hope he will launch an immediate investigation. 1 find it very stange that the courts did not insist that CN Telecommunications provide a full and clear explanation of why Mr. Maguire was dismissed.
In view of this the union decided to appeal to the Supreme Court of Ontario to reverse the decision of the arbitrator. This court upheld the arbitrator's decision. On December 21, 1976 the case was heard by the Ontario Court of Appeal and was dismissed on that day.
Legal counsel for the union has advised against further action in the courts but advises that the case be pursued in the "political arena".
So we are now pursuing this man's case in the political arena this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, and I certainly hope that the Minister of Justice will take some action on it.
We appeal to the members of parliament to correct this injustice. We are asking only that Mr. Bernie Maguire be given the specific reason for being denied his security clearance.
If CN Telecommunications has a clear cut, logical explanation why this man was dismissed, then he is certainly entitled to hear it. One reason we need this kind of bill and a commission is to investigate cases like this. The letter concludes:
Do we live in a country where the rights of an individual can be so trampled on that a person can be fired from his job and be branded for life as a "security risk" with no reasons given and no avenue of appeal?
The matter is in your hands. Please don't let us down.
This letter is signed by a number of his colleagues in the union, and the case is one example of an individual I should like to see helped. It is unfortunate that this human rights commission will not be established until about another two years, so I hope that the Minister of Justice will take some appropriate action.
I should like to give the House another example of what happened to some employees in another Crown corporation, Air Canada. Five Air Canada employees were wrongly charged in connection with the theft of gold at an airport in the state of New York. They incurred legal expenses amounting to $18,000 and the airline refused to compensate them for their financial losses even though they did in fact receive their back pay lost during their four months' suspension.
This is not an isolated incident, Mr. Speaker; rather it is one that seems to occur quite regularly. Perhaps there are many Crown corporation employees who do not fully realize the position they are in, and I will just explain why. We had another case of a gold theft at the Ottawa International Airport in April, 1975. Although this case has now been solved, Mr. Speaker, Air Canada employees who worked at the airport were under suspension. The same thing happened to them as happened to the Air Canada workers in New York.
The crux of the problem is the lax security measures at Air Canada terminals. This is not the fault of the employees. If Air Canada expects its employees to guard valuables, Air Canada should make the task easier by first stepping up its security measures and then it should take on the responsibility of paying the legal fees of those falsely accused of theft. If

they are placed in this vulnerable position, they should certainly be protected. There has been no decision with regard to paying the legal fees of these Air Canada employees falsely charged with theft. This is another group that can appear before the Human Rights Commission because they have been treated unjustly.
There are others who wish to speak on this bill this afternoon. Therefore I will not take any more time. As the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) stated, our party fully supports this bill. There are details that can be worked out in committee, and some improvements made. I welcomed the opportunity to enter this debate this afternoon.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at a time when basic individual rights are constantly jeered at in most countries of the world, the spirit if not the letter of the International Declaration on Human Rights remains ineffective, in spite of the nobility of the feelings by which it was prompted. I am grateful to the minister for that legislation which will legally ratify what is already found in the provincial jurisdictions and will enable Canada to join the unfortunately select club of nations which are not satisfied with pious and hollow words when time comes to deal with discrimination.
It is not sufficient, Mr. Speaker, to endorse the principle of a national, interjurisdictional or even international statement of rights, since concrete pledges to which it gives rise often contain pointless restrictions which deprive those rights of any real meaning and governments can then with impunity under the guise of national security or another wrong or hyperbolic reasoning cast them aside, alleging their temporary character. However, that feat of strength shows the weakness of those rights and the necessity of incorporating them in a statement and explaining grounds for discrimination while establishing an enforcement body to act as watch-dog ready to detect possible abuses by governments or individuals.
Therefore, principles and statements of intentions are important, but experience clearly shows that they are not enough and that solid structures must be developed to translate them concretely into facts and that solid tools must be developed to ensure that they are respected. That is the objective of Bill C-25, an Act to extend the present laws in Canada that proscribe discrimination and that protect the privacy of individuals.
This is an important step in the total process involved in implementing an articulated Canadian policy for the protection of human rights, but it is not the ultimate expression of this process since human activities related to this area are innumerable and the list of the abuses involved nearly endless. I hope that this is only the start of a dialogue which will find its extension in the study by the human rights protection commission and future discussions in the House, since the House will periodically evaluate any change in the situation. In this context which is somewhat vague, I admit, but neverthe-
February 11, 1977

less very tangible in what directly affects certain Canadians who are now the victims of discrimination, Bill C-25 will aim at correcting the weaknesses which are the most obvious and the most socially unacceptable in discriminatory practices without ending completely all discrimination among human beings.
Unfortunately, and in spite of the beauty of the concept of human brotherhood, as long as there will be a humanity, there will be discrimination. But it is precisely the role of society to protect itself from it and eventually eliminate it by establishing general policies from which it must not deviate while strictly defining the limits of its intervention and action so as to protect effectively, without interfering with, the expression of the most basic of rights, that of freedom of thought, individually and collectively.
Bill C-25, as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) and the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) have said so well, is a valid working paper with technical aspects that can eventually be reshaped and refined during the detailed study by the parliamentary Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. I will therefore postpone at this point some hopefully constructive criticisms that can better await the committee stage, in the light of the minister's commitment to reconsider the details of this proposal.
The bill is in five parts with a preamble stating the purpose of the legislation and its basic principles. These are that every individual should have an equal opportunity with other individuals to make for himself or herself the life that he or she is able and wishes to have, without being hindered in or prevented from doing so by discriminatory practices based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, age, sex or marital status, or conviction for an offence for which a pardon has been granted or by discriminatory employment practices based on physical handicap. As I said, there is a recognition of the need to strike a delicate balance between the rights of the individual and those of the community, in the statement that the privacy of individuals should be protected to the greatest extent consistent with public order and well-being.
I am somewhat astonished that in his speech the minister avoided any reference to the protection of the individual's language, because this is a basic right deserving special protection, as indicated in Section 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. I find no mention of it in the proscribed grounds of discrimination as stated in Bill C-25. I very much expect the minister can explain in due time to the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs and the Canadian public why he rejected that right, at least in this bill to extend the present laws in Canada that proscribe discrimination and that protect the privacy of individuals, and what he envisages as a substitute to the protection embodied in this legislation.
I realize that sufficient protection might be afforded by the insertion, in the preamble to the Canadian constitutional statutes commonly referred to as the Canadian Constitution, of a specific reference to the right of Canadians to communicate with the Canadian government in one of Canada's official languages. But what about the many Canadians whose mother
Canadian Human Rights Act
tongue is neither French nor English? There is something to think about although in every day practice it would be very hard to distinguish between outright discrimination on purely linguistic grounds and normal linguistic restrictions necessary to the orderly operation of Canadian society, more specifically of course in the area of unemployment.
Finally, let us remember that several members are expecting explanations and alternatives in this area from the minister. The creation of a Canadian Human Rights Commission is the natural extension of the statement of proscribed grounds of discrimination. Indeed, it is primordial to provide for the formation of a politically and administratively independent body whose object would be to sanction the contents of this legislation by looking for and into patent cases of discrimination. It was also very important that this commission should have extended powers, and clause 22 in that respect overwhelms me since in addition to the nearly police like aspect of its action in its role as a watch dog against proscribed discriminatory actions as set forth under Part I it may also undertake any action likely to promote collectively and socially the just cause of respect for all basic rights.
I hope in that sense that the commission will have great public exposure and that it will build around its work an aura of justice and equity, a sort of a secular arm of the equalitari-an social aspirations of our community. I will go quickly over Part III which also takes a look at discriminatory practices such as depriving an individual in Canada of government services to which he would normally be entitled, or adverse differentiation upon the provision of services.
Part IV deals with the protection of personal rights. This is an area about which a lot was written recently as it is related to the broader area of the right to information. The only thing covered here is an individual's access to government files compiled on him, and as many others I will be looking forward to an explicit line of conduct on what should be a unified and coherent policy on the right of the people of Canada to information and, correlatively, the classification of papers and documents produced by the government.
As for the protection of privacy of individuals, it is another of these fundamental rights that modern society has rediscovered after decades of systematic hesitation by governmental, semi-public, private and even sometimes secret agencies. Time has come indeed for us to issue, within the limits of the government's responsibility for collecting and processing individual data for federal information banks, strict rules enabling individuals to consult and, when required, correct the information stored about them. It is a very commendable objective whose sole foreseen restrictions, which I think will be very far reaching, would eventually inhibit its realizations by creating problems and conflicts of interest between the individual and the community in general.
In committee I intend to explore with the minister the extent and application of the anticipated restrictions and the right to information in order to establish with him and with our colleagues if, yes or no, we might be recognizing this right and at the same time strangling it by imposing overly severe

February 11, 1977
Canadian Human Rights Act
restrictions. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I will simply add that the bill is very valid and that its objectives are no doubt shared by all Canadians and a fortiori by all members of the House. As for the different clauses, they will be studied where we discuss such things, in committee. For the moment we are discussing the principle behind the bill and, like everyone else here, I consider that this principle has already been established.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this legislation has been ldng awaited and, as hon. members have said, there may be some difficulty in getting it to a level which we think would answer the best needs of Canadians as a whole.
We know that in the various provinces there are acts covering human rights, with some of the provinces, if not all, having human rights commissions. We have heard of some rather sensational cases and we have heard of others where, frankly, the commissions have got themselves in a snarl. I am concerned here about the danger of overlapping and that we would get varying standards between the federal legislation and that applicable to the provinces. I do not think one could say that it would be in any way tolerable, even less logical, to have differing standards of human rights in this country, regardless in which province the citizen or the resident may be located.
I would like to look briefly at some of the problems which I think must be encountered in some of the applications of human rights legislation by some of the provincial commissions. I think there is a very grave danger of discrimination in reverse. We have seen, particularly in the service industries, employers who have a particular purpose and who have a particular type of business in which a certain type of person must be employed, being denied the right to advertise, for instance, for a French chef. That is a no-no. Presumably one has to do it by way of advertising for a chef, either male or female, with a knowledge of French cuisine, and regardless of who may come up, in that particular type of establishment that person should have the right to that position. He may be completely unsuitable in the atmosphere or the type of restaurant or hotel that might be contemplated.
I was discussing this matter with manpower officials in Alberta with regard to the introduction into Canada under a work permit of, say, a Chinese chef of a particular type, whether he is skilled in Mandarin Chinese or Cantonese Chinese, whether he is a pastry cook, or what have you. One runs into the difficulty of saying you cannot specify that, you cannot say that you are going to put a Chinese cook in a Chinese restaurant. I say that is all a lot of poppycock because if the establishment is a Chinese restaurant, then in the kitchen there will be Chinese who understand the foods and who understand one another. To say that one should admit a person of other racial origin, who would be introduced, bulldozed or ramroded into one of these establishments, is totally wrong. That is one difficulty. It has already occurred and it
(Mr. Lachance.]
might, unfortunately, happen under legislation of this kind which in itself is very well meaning but which in its application is sometimes less than logical. Thus we get negative results. All that this can be called is discrimination in reverse, or inverse discrimination.
The third difficulty-and here I come back to the Department of Manpower and Immigration-is that in our present regulations the point system is discriminatory and certainly in principle and in spirit is contradictory to this act. Hon. members know that under the point system a person up to the age of 35 has no disabilities imposed upon him or her by reason of age, but any prospective immigrant over the age of 35 has one point deducted from the points obtained up to a maximum of ten. In other words, persons 45 years of age and over to the age of 65 have ten points deducted from the point score they have obtained, all because of age.
I say that the government of Canada in its application of its own immigration rules is engaged in a blatant form of discrimination with regard to the age indicated in this bill. Of course it may be that some of the purists or, to be more accurate, some of the legalists, will say "But in the act under clauses 5, 6, 7 and 8 immigration is not a subject in which discrimination is prohibited." I will say that perhaps it is something we should discuss in committee. Clause 8 reads:
It is a discriminatory practice ...
(ii) to make any written or oral inquiry that expresses or implies any
limitation, specification or preference based on a prohibited ground of
discrimination
I suggest to you that maybe the insistence on the point system with regard to age in a written or oral inquiry is a prohibited ground of discrimination. This is something that I will not discuss with the minister but he might want to take a look at it and inquire from his colleague, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), as to the existing and intended practice in the devising and application of regulations relative to the point system under the Immigration Act.
The next point I want to talk about is that perhaps one can justify it and say there is no discrimination in the two tier system of post-secondary education fees. It is said that this applies to all known Canadian residents whether they are landed immigrants or Canadian citizens. However, we should face the fact that the public clamour in some areas of Canada seeking to impose higher levels of fees on foreign students is nothing more or less then outright racism.
Far too many people have told me that they have seen people going around our university campuses who are not white, and it is for that reason that Canadians are being excluded from what they would consider easy admission to university courses, whether their averages are worthy of it or not, or whether their scholastic performance is worthy of it or not. Usually if a close inquiry is made, it is found that the academic standards were simply not high enough. However, these self-same people lump in as foreign students many Canadian born students who are of second or third generation
February 11, 1977

but whose skin does not happen to be white. They are all lumped together as foreign students, and the attitude is that they must be kept out. I say shame on all of it. I think that is a wrong principle. Where it has been used I think it has been wrong, and it has been used by the government of the province where this is being done.
After all, 85 per cent of the cost at university level is borne by the public purse. About 10 per cent of the cost is covered by tuition fees, and 5 per cent by grants, bursaries and scolar-ships. However, of that 85 per cent-and this is where some of the provincial legislatures are loath to come clean with the people-50 per cent comes from the coffers of the government of Canada. Granted, it comes from Canadian taxpayers all across the country. One of the reasons this country is suffering in this particular regard is the absence of a national educational policy. There are many reasons-but that is another subject-why there should be a national educational policy. However, this is one of the consequences of its absence.
Three years ago the universities were crying because they did not have enough students, but now when there is a problem of some crowding I do not think we should impose a two tier system of fees. The fact that it is done in some jurisdictions in the United States does not make it any more right. Perhaps I am subjective because it was my privilege to spend three years at a university in a country outside Canada. There was no distinction as to where I came from with regard to fees. I hope that the university life there was better for that policy. 1 certainly benefited from the presence of many foreign students, and I know that in Canadian universities the presence of foreign students benefits both the student body and the faculty, in the same way as does the use of foreign teachers. The alternative is intellectual incestuousness.
I am wondering whether the two tier system of university fees is not in contravention of at least the spirit of clause 5 of this bill, because it seems to me that the provision of education is the provision of a service. There is a differentiation "adversely in relation to any individual on a prohibited ground of discrimination", and that is of national or ethnic origin or race. I hope that those who seek to impose two tier systems of fees at universities will be dealt with in this bill. I will admit that there have been some arguments made, but in essence they must yield to the other arguments for treating all applicants to universities alike, whether they are at the under graduate or post graduate level.
Then there is a final area, and that is the area of labour relations. The hon. member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) made reference to unions. Many years ago I proposed motions, and I actually proposed an amendment to the Canada Labour Code which would prohibit the firing of a person who held bona fide religious beliefs against participation in a labour union. There are thousands of these people here in Canada, and there have been desultory efforts in Manitoba and Ontario-and there may now be in Saskatchewan-to bring in provisions to allow these people to engage in their chosen employment notwithstanding the fact that there is a closed union shop; that is, that those people who have a bona fide belief, as I indicated, will be
Canadian Human Rights Act
able to continue in their employment, notwithstanding that there is a closed union shop agreement, by paying the equivalent of full union dues to a charity which is mutually agreed upon by the union local and the individual concerned. There is no free ride in so far as non-payment of dues is concerned, but I suggest that there has been blatant discrimination on the basis of religious beliefs as a result of the implementation in many provinces of clauses under closed shop agreements.
The formula 1 have suggested has been tried. There may be other suggestions, but let it not be said that because of any type of labour agreement a person in Canada shall be kept out of his or her chosen employment by reason of religious beliefs.
The last point I wish to make refers to the Immigration Act. Persons presently in Canada under a minister's permit so that they may be able to work and get medicare and other benefits, are issued a social insurance number in the series nine. That is a clear indication to employers today that the status of this person as a citizen or immigrant is unsure. I have been advised by persons holding such cards that they must take jobs at lower than the going rate and that there are various forms of victimization as a result. Why must they have that series nine designation? As soon as the landing is cleared a new card is issued with a non-identifiable number. Mr. Speaker, that identifiable number is like the mark of Cain, and it should not apply.
There are many other areas of concern. We could talk about prejudice and so on, but these are the areas in which there is discrimination by reason of race, ethnic origin, maybe colour, religion, age and other things. I hope we will be able to discuss them with a degree of objectivity with the minister and his officials. If there is anything that will help passage of this legislation it will be the flexibility of the minister and his officials to accept ideas from the opposition and backbenchers. The front bench and its immediate advisers has no copyright on commonsense, logic and justice.

moved that Bill C-256, to amend the Criminal Code (counterfeit of rare coins and notes), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have often seen the Chair come to a very rapid understanding of matters in the House and I want to congratulate Your Honour for reading the mind of this Chamber and knowing we had agreed to proceed at this time with Bill C-256, an act to amend the Criminal Code (counterfeit of rare coins and notes).
I intend to be very brief, Mr. Speaker, but I should like to take the time of hon. members to outline the background of the bill and tell members about the support it has received.
Currently it is legal to buy, sell and own counterfeit copies of obsolete coins, non-legal tender coins. The Criminal Code in section 406 defines counterfeit moneys to mean counterfeits of current coins and current paper moneys that are the lawful coin of this country or elsewhere. Under present Canadian law a counterfeit coin may be produced if the government which issued it has expired, for example the Third Reich in Germany, or ancient Rome, or if in the country of origin that money is not received any longer as legal tender.
Part X of the Criminal Code, which deals with offences relating to currency, is intended to protect the money circulating in this country, whether foreign or Canadian. When the relevant section was enacted, the intention was not to protect the value of rare coins. However, Mr. Speaker, some coins have acquired a very high value and it is difficult to convict a counterfeiter or someone buying and selling counterfeit coins, because at present it is legal to own, buy or sell such counterfeit coins.
A lawyer who administers the hobby protection act in the United States when testifying at the hearings before that act was passed said that some fraudulent coins have been sold as originals. He gave as an illustration one importer who, in a few years prior to 1973, sold 40,000 coins as originals. All his shipments consisted of imitation coins, none of which was marked as a replica. Inexperienced persons are particularly easy to dupe when dealing with counterfeit coins. This practice causes problems for generations, and threatens the historical and exchange value of the originals.
It should be illegal to manufacture counterfeit coins without the word "copy" on them. This would protect collectors, investors, speculators and hoarders. With the word "copy" clearly embossed, it would be obvious that the coins are not meant to be used as currency. The market in gold and silver coins is estimated to be many millions of dollars. What is needed, and what is proposed, is a law to protect collectors from fraudulent non-current coins.

February 11, 1977

It is common practice in Italy and Lebanon, and was until recently in Germany and some other places, to counterfeit coins as long as they are not current coins. Mints in those countries are actively engaged in manufacturing such coins. With modern technology and methods, the counterfeiters are turning out copies of very valuable coins which cannot be distinguished from the originals; these are copies not only of obsolete coins, but even copies of Canadian $5 and $10 gold pieces of 1912, 1913 and 1914, as well as of Canadian silver dollars of the 1930's and 1940's. These are listed in price lists as counterfeits, mailed all over Canada and the United States by counterfeiters, if I may call them that, and sold at just over the metal value. These counterfeit coins are so good that is often impossible to tell the difference between them and the legal ones. In fact the counterfeit ones quite often look more authentic. Although they are advertised as counterfeit coins by the manufacturer, unscrupulous buyers can pass them off as originals, and this is being done frequently. These counterfeit coins also find their way into bazaars in Europe and then into our own country. There are literally millions in circulation.
In 1973 the United States passed its hobby protection act which made it unlawful to manufacture, import, introduce into business or distribute any imitation numismatic item, coin, paper money, token or medal, which is not plainly and permanently marked "copy". The act is both criminal and civil. It permits any person to commence civil action for an injunction and damages wherever the defendant has an office or home. It makes it illegal to bring a counterfeit coin into the country unless it is stamped "copy". This legislation was enacted ten months after being brought to the attention of Congress. I am told it has worked very well.
West Germany in January, 1975, enacted a similar law which prohibits the manufacture of unmarked reproductions. This law was passed a few months after members of the Vancouver Institute of Coin Enthusiasts and the Montreal Numismatics Society presented petitions to the German ambassador in Canada. This organization in Canada can take much credit for the enactment of the law by the West German government.
Mine is a short bill, Mr. Speaker, and has already been widely circulated in the country. It was referred to in the trade magazine, the collector's magazine and the numismatists' magazine. I have also received letters, which I should like to present to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, from the Canadian Association of Numismatic Dealers, signed by Mr. A1 Bliman, executive secretary; from the Canadian Paper Money Society, signed by Mr. W. H. McDonald as past president; and from the Canadian Numismatic Association, signed by the president, Mr. Alex L. Munro. As those letters show, those three organizations representing the major numismatic associations of Canada support the principle of the legislation. In one letter it is suggested that the size of the word "copy" should be somewhat different from that proposed in my bill. In any event, the technical aspects of the bill, matters of size, type, etc., can more properly be con-

One other thing. I hope the hon. member will forgive me for importing it into the debate but I believe it is relevant to the subject matter. Members of parliament, including members of the Senate, now travel rather widely under the auspices of the Speaker of the House and the Speaker of the Senate. We visit other countries. We receive many delegations from other countries. This year I think the habit has been that we present those delegates with souvenirs of the 1976 Olympics. It has been the habit for us to give Olympic coins.
It happened yesterday when the Speaker presented the Speaker of the Venezuelan House of Representatives with a gold Olympic coin, a very treasured thing. But if that is a treasured gift to give and to receive, I think we ought to consider the striking of a parliamentary medallion which would be reserved for use by the Speakers and the heads of delegations visiting foreign countries under the auspices of one of our parliamentary associations. Such a medallion could be given to the other delegation, perhaps replicas or miniatures to members in the House, and we would also do the same to visitors to our parliament who come here under the auspices of other parliaments to visit in an official capacity as parliamentarians.
I have been in this House since 1972. There are some in this Chamber who were in the House before that time. Some were
here a long time before that time. Some have been here only since 1974. As a Canadian, I am very proud to be a member of this parliament. I know that all members in this House are proud to be members of parliament. Whether we sit here for a long time or a short time depends on a number of factors, but we are all of us proud to be members of parliament. We are proud of these buildings.
We are proud of the traditions which are part of this institution. It is an institution which is changing, but I do not think it is too much to suggest that we could exhibit that pride by some striking medallion which could be presented in the way I suggested, and under the auspices which I suggested, and which would be a visible reminder to our visitors, a visible reminder to our hosts, of our pride in this institution. I hope this idea will gain support from members on both sides of the House of Commons and in all parties and that Your Honour would convey my feelings to the Speaker of the House of Commons and that he, in turn, would convey them to the Speaker of the Senate.
I know we would have to examine the technical details and a host of other things, but in principle I believe it is important that we exhibit as members of parliament, in the broad sense in which we use the word parliament, our pride in belonging to this institution, our pride in taking part, for a long time or a short time, in the national life, and participating in debates in this place. And given the fact there is a certain importance attached to this authorized travel, in having the world understand our country, and in understanding the rest of the world and people in other parts of the world who are engaged in exactly the same practices, people who are now, hopefully, under free and democratic parliaments, but perhaps even some who are not so free and democratic, we should adopt this bill being put forward by the hon. member today, and consider in the long term sending a message to the Speakers of both Houses asking them to study my suggestion in consultation with the House leaders. I think this is a very important thing.
I hope I have not impinged on the courtesy of the hon. member in discussing his bill and that he will not feel hurt that I import this into a speech, but I want to congratulate him on bringing forward his bill and let him know he has my support.

Hopefully I will not be. Hopefully I will be in the House of Commons in another place. Before entering into a discussion on the merits of Bill C-256, I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate my seatmate, the hon. member for York Centre and the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Kaplan) for his initiative on behalf of numismatists and other coin collectors who have been defrauded in the past. At present the Criminal Code definition of counterfeit money does not include numismatic counterfeits. This is so because section 406 as it relates to coins requires that the coin in question be "current". "Current" means that the coins must be lawful currency in Canada or elsewhere by virtue of a law, proclamation or regulation in force in Canada or elsewhere, as the case may be.
Section 406(a) provides that a false coin is counterfeit if it resembles or is intended to resemble a current coin. The numismatic coins that the proposed amendment is designed to cover do not resemble "current" coins. They are designed to resemble genuine rare coins that may have been current at one time but no longer are. In fact it has been argued that the "fake" numismatic coins are not false in that they have as much if not more gold, silver or nickel content than the original coins have.
Section 406(e), likewise, does not apply. It provides that a coin cased with gold, silver or nickel is counterfeit if it is intended to resemble or pass for current gold, silver or nickel coin. Again, this section does not apply since the authentic numismatic coins are not current. The same reasoning applies to counterfeit paper notes. They must also be current.
There is no specific provision in the code to cover numismatic counterfeits. It may be that a criminal fraud or an obtaining by false pretence charge may be laid if the vendor of these coins or notes represents them to a purchaser as authentic. The Crown would be required to establish beyond a reasonable doubt that the vendor actually knew that the coins were not authentic. Subjective knowledge is extremely difficult to prove.
It clearly is not an offence if a person manufactures a replica coin or note that is not current.

If I may continue quoting from my memo, it clearly is not an offence if a person manufactures a replica coin or note that is not current. If the code were to be amended to prevent this temptation from arising, then the number of frauds involving counterfeit numismatic coins or notes should be substantially reduced.
